text: Given an array of strings called strs, group the anagrams together. Return the groups in any order.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — two strings are anagrams if they have the same letters with the same counts, just reordered, like eat and tea. Are these all lowercase English letters, and can there be empty strings or duplicates?
Lowercase only, lengths up to one hundred, and yes — empty strings are possible.

Key observation: two strings are anagrams if and only if their sorted forms are identical. So the sorted string is a canonical fingerprint for a whole anagram group. Example: eat, tea, tan, ate, nat, bat. A-e-t collects eat, tea and ate; a-n-t collects tan and nat; a-b-t collects bat. Three groups.

Let me think about how to group efficiently. Comparing every pair for anagram-ness is N squared times L — too slow at N equals ten to the fourth. This problem reminds me of hash grouping by a canonical key: compute each string's sorted form as a key and bucket into a hash map. Anagrams collide into the same bucket automatically.

Here's the plan. One: make a map from sorted key to the list of original words. Two: for each word, sort a copy to get its key, and push the word into that bucket. Three: return all the buckets. One thing worth flagging — I sort a copy for the key and push the original word into the bucket, so the output keeps the input strings intact. A trade-off worth mentioning — sorting the key is L log L. I could instead use a twenty-six-letter count as the key for linear time per word, giving N times L overall. For L up to one hundred, the sorted key is simpler and plenty fast, but I'd switch to counts if strings were long. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Let me write the sorted-key version. One pass builds the buckets: copy the word, sort the copy, and append the original under that key. A second loop collects every bucket into the answer. The line that's easy to get wrong is string key equals w — sorting w itself would put scrambled letters into the output instead of the real words. Both loops take the word and the bucket by value, so they copy; that's fine at this size.

Let's dry-run eat, tea, tan, ate, nat, bat. The row that matters is ate: its sorted key, a-e-t, already exists from eat and tea, so it joins that bucket instead of starting a new one — that's the hash map doing the grouping. Bat opens a third key. Final groups: eat, tea, ate; tan, nat; and bat. Corner cases: a single empty string gives one group holding the empty string, since empty sorts to empty. A single a gives one group of a. All identical strings land in one bucket. All check out.

Time is N times L log L — N words, each sorted in L log L. Space is N times L — every word plus its key stored in the map. The count-key variant drops time to N times L. One more thing — this is the general canonical-fingerprint-plus-hash-grouping pattern. If the alphabet weren't fixed lowercase, I'd prefer the sorted key, since a twenty-six-slot count array wouldn't apply.
Nicely done. Three things stood out: the sorted-form fingerprint framing, keying on a copy while pushing the original, and knowing when the count-key trade-off actually matters. Good work.
